terms.meaning: "Earth-shaped": flattened at the poles and bulging at the equator. Also called an oblate spheroid.
The network made where latitude and longitude lines cross at right angles.
An imaginary line joining places at the same angular distance north or south of the equator.
An imaginary line from pole to pole that crosses the equator at a right angle.
Another name for longitude: "meri" (mid) and "dian" (day), as places on it share noon.
Time by the Sun's position at a place: 12 noon when the Sun is overhead there.
One uniform time for a whole country, from its central meridian.

items.name: Names of the Earth
items.formula: Living Planet, Unique Planet, Watery Planet and Blue Planet.
items.example: It is the third planet from the Sun and the fifth largest.

items.name: Land and water on Earth
items.formula: Total 510 million sq km: water 361 million (70.78%), land 149 million (29.22%).
items.example: The land to water ratio is 1 : 2.43.

items.name: Earth's two diameters
items.example: The difference of 42 km is the proof that the Earth is a geoid.

items.name: Continents
items.formula: 7: Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe and Australia.
items.example: Asia is the largest and Australia the smallest.

items.name: Oceans
items.example: Pacific: largest and deepest. Arctic: smallest and shallowest.

items.name: Land and Water Hemispheres
items.formula: North: 60% land, 40% water. South: 81% water, 19% land.
items.example: That is why the North is the Land Hemisphere.

items.name: The equator
items.formula: 0° latitude, the longest line, called the Great Circle.
items.example: Other latitudes get shorter away from it.

items.name: Number of latitudes
items.formula: 90 on each side plus the equator makes 181.
items.example: Two degrees of latitude are 110.4 km apart on the ground.

items.name: Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn
items.example: Both are the same distance from the equator.

items.name: Arctic and Antarctic Circles
items.example: The poles are at 90° North and 90° South.

items.name: Prime Meridian
items.example: 180 lines east and 180 west make 360 longitudes.

items.name: How far apart longitudes are
items.formula: 111 km at the equator, less towards the poles, where they meet.
items.example: All longitudes are the same length.

items.name: East gains, West loses
items.formula: East of Greenwich add the time; west of it subtract.
items.example: At 12 noon GMT, a place 30° East of Greenwich has 2 pm.

items.name: Indian Standard Time
items.formula: Based on 82°30' East, which passes through Prayagraj.
items.example: 82.5 × 4 = 330 minutes, so IST is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of GMT.

items.name: Time zones
items.formula: The globe has 24, each 1 hour apart.
items.example: Russia 11, USA and Canada 5 each, Australia 3.

items.name: International Date Line
items.formula: Along the 180° meridian in the Pacific, with detours around land.
items.example: Crossing it west to east you repeat a day; east to west you lose one.

mistakes.text: Latitudes run east-west and get shorter away from the equator. Longitudes run pole to pole and are all equal in length.
Moving east, add time. Moving west, subtract. Don't reverse them.
West to east across the date line gains a day; going east to west loses one. It's the opposite of what many guess.
